readerTitle: Why Walmart chose small towns over big cities
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Walmart 초기 확장 전략) + 가상 적용 (상업용 청소 회사, 사내 계약 검토팀)
insight: 규모 해자는 회사가 큰 것이 아니라, 특정 시장 안에서 경쟁자보다 고정비를 더 많은 고객에게 나눠 지는 것이다.
misconception: 전국적으로 더 큰 회사가 어디서든 비용 우위를 가진다. 몸집이 크면 그 자체로 방어벽이 된다.

sources.text: Walton, S. with Huey, J. (1992). Sam Walton: Made in America. Doubleday.
Greenwald, B. & Kahn, J. (2005). Competition Demystified. Portfolio.
Ghemawat, P. (1986). Wal-Mart Stores' Discount Operations. Harvard Business School case.
청소 회사와 사내 계약팀 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Walmart 첫 매장은 1962년 아칸소주 로저스에서 열렸습니다. 게시 전 회사 공식 연혁으로 다시 확인하세요.
물류센터에서 하루 운전 거리 안에 매장을 모아 짓는 전략, 작은 도시 공략은 Walton(1992)과 Ghemawat(1986)에 나옵니다. 카드에는 정확한 거리나 매장 수를 적지 않았습니다.
'매장이 밀집한 지역에서 우위가 가장 컸다'는 주장은 Greenwald & Kahn(2005)의 분석을 일반적으로 요약한 것입니다. 구체적 수익률 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다. 원문 표현을 확인하세요.
가상 계산: 도시 하나의 고정비(감독자, 차량, 장비, 영업) 월 $20,000. 고객 40곳이면 $20,000 ÷ 40 = $500, 고객 5곳이면 $20,000 ÷ 5 = $4,000. 차이 8배.

cards.title: Why Walmart chose small towns over big cities
body: In its early decades, Walmart did something that looked small-minded. While big discount chains fought over large cities, it kept opening stores in small towns in the American South.
Many of those towns could support only one big discount store. That choice says a lot about what size really protects.

image.label: Map with a tight cluster of small stores around one warehouse
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일 지도. 창고 하나를 중심으로 작은 매장 여러 개가 촘촘히 모여 있고, 멀리 큰 도시에는 다른 매장들이 흩어져 경쟁하는 모습. 실제 로고, 상표, 매장 간판은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A giant enters your city.
body: You run a commercial cleaning company with 40 office clients in one city. A national cleaning firm, ten times your size overall, opens a branch here and signs its first 5 clients.
In this city, who has the cost advantage?

options.text: The national firm. It buys supplies in bulk and has a bigger name
options.feedback: Bulk buying helps a little, but supplies are a small share of cleaning costs. The big costs here are local, and locally the national firm is tiny.

options.text: You. Your crews, vans and supervisors are spread over 40 nearby clients
options.feedback: Right. The costs that don't change with each client are shared eight times more widely on your side. The next cards show why.

options.text: Neither. Cleaning is labor, so size doesn't matter
options.feedback: True that labor scales with work. But supervisors, vans, route time and sales effort don't, and those decide who can price lower.

cards.title: Fill one region before moving to the next.
body: Sam Walton opened the first Walmart in Rogers, Arkansas, in 1962. Instead of spreading across the country, the company filled in regions. Stores clustered within a day's drive of a distribution center.
One warehouse, one truck fleet and one regional team served many stores. Each new store in the cluster made those shared costs cheaper per store.
A rival entering one of those towns had to carry its own trucks and warehouse for a single store, in a town too small for two.

cards.title: Scale as a moat
body: **Scale becomes a moat** when a business has large fixed costs, meaning costs that don't grow with each customer, and it spreads them over more customers than rivals in the same market.
Its cost per customer is lower, so it can charge less and still profit. A newcomer must win a big share of the market to catch up, and it loses money while it tries.

image.label: Same fixed cost bar split into many slices versus few slices
image.brief: 같은 길이의 막대 두 개. 왼쪽은 40조각으로 잘게 나뉘어 한 조각이 얇고, 오른쪽은 5조각으로 나뉘어 한 조각이 두꺼움. 라벨 "Same fixed cost", "40 customers", "5 customers". 로고 없음.

cards.title: Back to the cleaning company.
body: Say each city branch needs $20,000 a month for supervisors, vans, equipment and sales, no matter how many offices it cleans. The giant is ten times your size nationally, yet here it pays **eight times more** per client.

cards.title: The size that counts is local.
body: Scale only protects you in the market where your fixed costs are shared. Analysts such as Bruce Greenwald have argued that Walmart's advantage was strongest where its stores were densest, and weaker far from its home regions.
So the useful question is not "Are we big?" It's "In which market are we bigger than anyone, and do fixed costs matter there?"
cards.softwareNote: Software is mostly fixed cost: building and running the product costs about the same for 1,000 users or 10,000. The moat comes from being the largest player in a specific niche, not from total headcount or funding.

cards.title: Three ways scale stops protecting you.
list: **The market grows:** a bigger market leaves room for a second player to reach your scale
**Fixed costs shrink:** new tools or rented services let small rivals match your costs
**You spread thin:** chasing size in new markets means being small everywhere
cards.callout: A moat built on scale needs a market that stays limited and costs that stay fixed.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a company.
body: You lead an in-house contracts team that reviews supplier contracts for eight divisions. You've built templates, a clause library and trained reviewers. One division head wants to hire an outside law firm instead.
How do you make your team hard to replace?

options.text: Take on every kind of legal work for any division, so the team looks bigger
options.feedback: You'd grow, but in areas where you're small and the law firm is deep. Your cost advantage would get diluted.

options.text: Go deeper on the contract types all eight divisions share, and speed them up
options.feedback: Your templates and tools are spread across more of this company's contracts than any outside firm handles. That's where your cost per contract is lowest.

options.text: Offer that one division a lower internal charge
options.feedback: It may keep the division for now. But a discount without a lower cost underneath is a price cut, not a moat.

cards.title: Scale protects you where you're bigger than everyone else.
body: Being large overall is not a moat. Sharing big fixed costs across more customers than any rival in one market is.
**Try it today:** list your three biggest fixed costs. For each, name the market where you share it across the most customers, and the rival closest to matching you there.
